volumes.title: The Fire Is Lit
volumes.text:
Emberwick, the loft above Bunce’s bakery in Cinder Lane, the first of January. I am Ambrose Thimblewick, alchemist, and today I began the Great Work as my late aunt’s book describes it.

The method is simple, which is what makes it hard. Into a crucible no bigger than a teacup I have put one grey pebble from the river Ember, three drops of rainwater that fell by moonlight, and a pinch of patience, which the book says cannot be bought and must be supplied by the operator. The lid goes on. The crucible sits on a brick ledge over a small fire.

For twelve months the fire must never go out and the lid must never be lifted. On the last night of the year the pebble will have ripened into gold. I have a sack of coal, a stool and a clock. It is now twenty past nine.

volumes.title: The Draught
volumes.text:
Cinder Lane, Emberwick, February. I am Ambrose Thimblewick, keeping a small fire under a small crucible in the loft above the bakery. If the fire burns for a year without a break, the pebble inside is to become gold.

At three this morning a draught came under the door like a cold cat and laid the flame flat. I stopped the gap with my second-best stockings and walked up and down until it stood again. Mrs. Bunce, the baker, sleeps beneath my floor until four. She came up to ask whether I was keeping a horse.

I explained the Work. She listened with her arms folded. “A year,” she said. “I cannot get this lane to wait while a loaf cools.” But she looked at the fire for some time before she went down, and at seven there was a warm roll on the top stair.

volumes.title: A Cat on the Lid
volumes.text:
The loft over Bunce’s bakery, Emberwick, March. Ambrose Thimblewick, alchemist. Third month of keeping one fire alight under one covered crucible, in the hope of gold at the year’s end.

The bakery cat, Crumpet, has found the warmest place in Cinder Lane, and it is the lid of my crucible. She arrives at dusk, turns round twice and settles on it like a tea cosy. I consulted the book. It forbids lifting the lid, letting the fire die, and “undue haste”. It says nothing on the subject of cats.

I have reasoned as follows. A cat is warm, steady and in no hurry, which is more than can be said for me. If patience is truly an ingredient, she is adding to the supply. I let her stay. She has now watched more hours of the Great Work than I have, and with a better temper.

volumes.title: One Red Coal
volumes.text:
Emberwick, Cinder Lane, April. I am Ambrose Thimblewick. Since New Year I have kept a fire under a crucible in my loft, for if it goes out before twelve months are up there will be no gold. Last night I fell asleep.

I woke at dawn with my cheek on the table and my heart in my boots. The fire was alive. Kneeling at the hearth was Tilly Bunce, the baker’s daughter, who is ten. She had come up for the cat and found one red coal and an alchemist snoring. She was feeding it wood shavings, one at a time, the way one feeds a sick sparrow.

I thanked her. She asked sensible questions about the pebble. Then she said she could watch from four until six, after school, if I wanted to sleep like other people. The Work has an assistant.

volumes.title: The Roster
volumes.text:
The loft above the bakery, Cinder Lane, Emberwick, May. Ambrose Thimblewick, alchemist, fifth month of tending a fire that must burn a full year beneath a closed crucible.

I caught a cold and could not get up the stairs with the coal. Tilly Bunce, my assistant, went down the lane knocking on doors. By evening there was a sheet of paper pinned to mine, ruled in pencil. Mr. Okey the cobbler has Tuesday nights, since he does not sleep anyway. Hetty Flagg the mason has Sunday mornings. Mrs. Bunce has put herself down for “before the ovens”. There are seven names, and until this week I knew two of them.

I lay in bed listening to strangers creak across my floor and put coal on my fire, more carefully than I do. It is an odd feeling for a solitary man. I cannot say I dislike it.

volumes.title: A Knot in the String
volumes.text:
Emberwick, the loft in Cinder Lane, midsummer. I am Ambrose Thimblewick, and for six months I and a roster of neighbours have kept a fire going under a small crucible. The lid stays on until the year’s end. Then, the book promises, gold.

Half-way is the dangerous time. This afternoon the loft was hot as an oven, and I found my hand resting on the lid. One look, I thought. The book would never know. Tilly Bunce, who is ten and watches from four until six, removed my hand, fetched string, and tied the lid down with a great many knots.

She says it is easier to be patient when there is a knot. That may be the truest sentence in alchemy. Half the lane sat on my stairs this evening, where there is a breeze, eating Mrs. Bunce’s buns. Nobody touched the string.

volumes.title: What the Cobbler Would Buy
volumes.text:
Cinder Lane, Emberwick, July. Ambrose Thimblewick, alchemist. Seven months ago I shut a river pebble in a crucible over a slow fire; in five more it is to be gold. My neighbours share the watching.

On Tuesday night Mr. Okey the cobbler asked what I would do with the gold. I opened my mouth and found little in it. Mend the roof. New stockings. After that I could not think. I had been so busy wanting gold that I had never asked it any questions.

So I asked him. He said that he would put a window in the east wall of his shop, to see the morning while he worked. Hetty Flagg wants a donkey. Mrs. Bunce wants one day in bed. Tilly wants the pebble, if it stays a pebble. I have written this on the back of the roster. It is a better list than mine.

volumes.title: Gold in a Fortnight
volumes.text:
The loft above Bunce’s bakery, Emberwick, August. I am Ambrose Thimblewick. With the help of Cinder Lane I am keeping a year-long fire under a crucible, as an old book directs, to turn a pebble into gold. Eight months are done.

A man came through town selling a pamphlet called Gold in a Fortnight. I bought one. I am not proud of it. It promised that no patience whatever was required, and I read it three times on the stairs.

Mrs. Bunce took it from me and read the first page. “Fortnight bread is poor bread,” she said. Mr. Okey the cobbler said fortnight boots were worse. Tilly asked who would have Tuesdays if I went over to the quick way. Then she used the pamphlet to light the evening coal. It burned very well, which is the only thing I can report in its favour.

volumes.title: A Crack in the Ledge
volumes.text:
Emberwick, Cinder Lane, September. Ambrose Thimblewick, alchemist, in the ninth month of a twelve-month fire. Over it sits a closed crucible that must not be opened, cooled or, I now add, dropped.

This morning the brick ledge under the crucible cracked across with a noise like a walnut. The whole thing tipped. I caught it in the tongs and stood there. I could not put it down, for there was nothing level to put it on, and I could not take it off the heat.

Tilly, the baker’s girl, ran for Hetty Flagg the mason, who came with a trowel and rebuilt the ledge under my arms while I held the crucible steady. It took two hours. Mr. Okey fed me a bun in pieces. When I set it down at last, the lane, which had gathered on the stairs, gave a cheer. My arms still shake as I write.

volumes.title: Thursday Suppers
volumes.text:
The loft over the bakery, Cinder Lane, Emberwick, October. I am Ambrose Thimblewick. A small crucible has sat over a fire here since New Year, watched in turns by me and my neighbours, and at the year’s end it is to hold gold.

Somewhere in the summer the watching turned into company. On Thursdays now everyone comes up with a dish. Mrs. Bunce brings a pie. Mr. Okey brings his fiddle and plays the two tunes he knows. There are fourteen names on the roster. Tonight old Mr. Larch, who has not left his room in two winters, climbed all my stairs to take his first watch.

He sat by the fire with Crumpet the cat on his knee and said it was the warmest he had been in years. I used to have one chair. I counted nine, and none of them is mine.

volumes.title: Doubts at Three O’Clock
volumes.text:
Cinder Lane, Emberwick, November. Ambrose Thimblewick, alchemist. Eleven months of fire under a covered crucible, with one to go. I shall write down a thing I have not said aloud.

I think it is a pebble. I think it was a pebble in January and will be a pebble at New Year, a warm one. I sat with that at three this morning and waited to feel wretched. Instead I found I was worrying about something else. When the lid comes off, the watching stops. Nobody will need Tuesdays.

Tilly Bunce came up at four. I told her my doubt, since she is my assistant. She thought about it while she put coal on. “We will see in a month,” she said. “And somebody has to keep the fire in anyway. It is winter.” I had not looked at it from that side.

volumes.title: The Lid Comes Off
volumes.text:
Emberwick, the loft above Bunce’s bakery, the last night of December. I am Ambrose Thimblewick. For a year, with all of Cinder Lane taking turns, I have kept a fire under a closed crucible that was to turn a river pebble into gold.

At midnight the stairs were full. Tilly cut the string. I lifted the lid with the tongs, and inside was a grey pebble. It was the same pebble, perhaps a little rounder. Nobody spoke. Then Mr. Okey asked whose turn it was on Tuesday, and Mrs. Bunce said hers, and Hetty Flagg said the ledge wanted looking at in spring.

So the roster stays on the door. Tilly took the pebble home in her mitten, and tells me it was still warm at breakfast. Result of the Great Work: no gold. One fire, still in. Fourteen names, and a year ago I knew two.

volumes.title: A Challenge by Carrier
volumes.text:
Saltmere, on the Grey Coast, January. To Dr. Ignatius Vole, at Cold Ashby in the Fells. Sir, I have read your piece in the Almanack, which states that all things are at bottom a Spirit. They are not.

I am Perpetua Marrow, alchemist, and I have twenty-three jars to prove that all things are at bottom a Salt. A Salt is what remains when the fuss has gone out of a thing. The old books say the perfect Salt will turn lead to gold. I say it will at least keep.

I enclose a jar by Mr. Tobble’s cart: Salt of Sea Fog. I gathered it by leaving a clean plate on the harbour wall through a grey morning. It is white, fine, and faintly mournful. Examine it honestly, then tell me a smell could do as much. I propose we settle the matter at Emberwick, at Midwinter.

volumes.title: Dr. Vole Replies
volumes.text:
Cold Ashby, in the Northern Fells, February. To Miss Perpetua Marrow, at Saltmere. Madam, your jar of Salt of Sea Fog arrived. So did a week of damp and melancholy in my study, which lifted only when my housekeeper, Mrs. Grice, carried the thing out to the scullery. She says she rather likes it. I do not consult Mrs. Grice on philosophy.

A Salt is what is left when everything interesting has departed. A Spirit, in our trade, is whatever rises: a steam, a scent, a breath. I am Ignatius Vole, and I have caught forty of them. I send one by the carrier, Spirit of First Thaw. I took it by holding a bottle under the eaves at the moment the roof sighed. Uncork it near a window.

Emberwick at Midwinter will suit. Bring your jars. I shall bring the truth, which travels lighter.

volumes.title: Salt of Old Arguments
volumes.text:
Saltmere, Grey Coast, March. To Dr. Vole, at Cold Ashby, from Perpetua Marrow, who holds that everything is at bottom a Salt, against his claim that everything is a Spirit.

Sir, I uncorked your Spirit of First Thaw. For one afternoon my kitchen smelled of wet slate and snowdrops, and the cat sat in the window as if expecting someone. It was not unpleasant. I withdraw that. It was a smell, and by supper it had gone, which is my whole point about Spirits.

By Mr. Tobble’s cart I send something that lasts: Salt of Old Arguments. I scraped it from the inside of a teapot that has stood between two sisters for forty years. It is brown and bitter to the nose, with a warmth afterwards that I cannot account for. Keep the lid on in company. We meet at Emberwick at Midwinter, and I advise you to prepare.

volumes.title: Spirit of Kettle
volumes.text:
Cold Ashby, Northern Fells, April. To Miss Marrow, at Saltmere, from Ignatius Vole, who maintains against her that all things are Spirits and not Salts.

Madam, I set your Salt of Old Arguments on my desk with the lid off, purely as a trial. Within the hour I had written to my brother at Barleyford, to whom I have not written in nine years. I mention this as a result and not as a kindness. He has replied. That is beside the point.

The carrier brings you Spirit of Kettle. It is the breath a kettle lets go just before it sings, and it took me eleven mornings to catch, since one must not be seen waiting. One question, for my records only. Is your coast as grey as reported? I have never seen the sea. Mrs. Grice, my housekeeper, says it is mostly weather.

volumes.title: The Empty Jar
volumes.text:
Saltmere, on the Grey Coast, May. To Dr. Vole, at Cold Ashby in the Fells, from Perpetua Marrow, keeper of Salts, to the keeper of Spirits.

Sir, the coast is grey the way a pigeon is grey, which is to say every colour if you stand still. Your Spirit of Kettle made my cold workroom feel as though someone had just left it to fetch cake. I send Salt of Tears, the laughing kind only, gathered at the fish market while Jem Scully told the story of the eel. I do not bottle the sorrowful kind. It does not keep, and ought not to.

Since you ask for records, here is one. My shelf holds twenty-three full jars and one empty. Its label reads Salt of Contentment. I have looked for that Salt for nineteen years and never found a grain. You need not reply to this part.

volumes.title: A House with One Chair
volumes.text:
Cold Ashby, in the Fells, June. To Miss Marrow, at Saltmere on the Grey Coast, from Dr. Ignatius Vole. We are in dispute, she for Salts, I for Spirits.

Madam, I shall reply to that part. I also keep an empty vessel. It is a small blue bottle marked Spirit of Good Company. I have held it open at fairs, at weddings and once at a sheep sale, and caught nothing. Mrs. Grice, my housekeeper, says it will never rise in a house with one chair. I did not ask her opinion.

I enclose Spirit of Hayfield at Noon, taken yesterday from the top of a wagon. Do not open it if you have work to finish. Your laughing Salt is on my windowsill, and I find I look at it. An empty jar is an honest thing to own. I had thought I was the only one.

volumes.title: An Accident in the Cart
volumes.text:
Saltmere, Grey Coast, July. To Dr. Vole, at Cold Ashby, from Perpetua Marrow. He says all things are Spirits; I say Salts; this letter concerns a mishap between the two.

Sir, your bottle of Hayfield at Noon cracked on the fell road. Mr. Tobble the carrier sneezed the whole way down and reports that he felt six years old as far as the marsh. That is not my complaint. The Spirit ran into the box where I was returning your empty jars, and one of them still had a pinch of my Sea Fog Salt in the bottom.

When I lifted the lid there was a cloud in the jar. It was the size of a plum, and it was raining. It rained for a minute on the bottom of the jar and then cleared. Neither a Salt nor a Spirit does that alone. I am very much annoyed.

volumes.title: A Cloud the Size of a Bun
volumes.text:
Cold Ashby, Northern Fells, August. To Miss Marrow, at Saltmere, from Ignatius Vole, her opponent in the question of Salts against Spirits.

Madam, I did not believe your cloud. I therefore dropped one pinch of your Salt of Sea Fog into an open bottle of my Spirit of Kettle, to prove you mistaken. A cloud the size of a bun formed above the inkstand. It rained on my notes for a full minute. Then it produced a rainbow no wider than my thumb, and went. I was extremely cross about the notes. I have since done it four more times. Mrs. Grice brings a saucer now.

I must set down, as a man of method, what I observed. Your Salt alone sits in its jar. My Spirit alone drifts off. Together they made weather. I do not yet know what this does to my position. Kindly send more fog.

volumes.title: A Comfortable Silence
volumes.text:
Saltmere, on the Grey Coast, September. To Dr. Vole at Cold Ashby, from Perpetua Marrow. For nine months we have argued by carrier’s cart whether the world is made of Salts, as I say, or of Spirits, as he does.

Sir, more fog is enclosed. I too have been trying things. Last night I let three breaths of your Spirit of First Thaw into my jar of Old Arguments. The jar grew warm in my hands. Then a silence came into the kitchen, the comfortable kind that sits between people who have finished quarrelling. It lasted until supper.

I have a proposal, and I make it with dignity. When we meet at Emberwick at Midwinter, let it be less a contest than a joint examination. We might each bring everything. I would bring the empty jar. You need not say yes at once. Say it by the next cart.

volumes.title: A Second Chair
volumes.text:
Cold Ashby, in the Fells, October. To Miss Marrow, at Saltmere, from Dr. Ignatius Vole. Our dispute, Salts against Spirits, was to be settled at Emberwick at Midwinter; she now proposes a joint examination.

Madam, yes. I say it with every reluctance I can muster, which I find is not much. I shall bring all forty Spirits and the blue bottle that has never held anything. I have not left Cold Ashby in eleven years. Mr. Tobble will take me down the fell road in his cart, and has promised to drive as if I were eggs.

I have also bought a second chair. It is for the study, in case of visitors. Mrs. Grice had to sit down in it. I enclose Spirit of Woodsmoke in October, for your own journey. Open it when the coast road turns inland. It is good company on a hill.

volumes.title: How You Will Know Me
volumes.text:
Saltmere, Grey Coast, November. To Dr. Vole, at Cold Ashby in the Northern Fells, from Perpetua Marrow, alchemist. Once his opponent on the matter of Salts and Spirits; now, it seems, his colleague in an examination at Emberwick next month.

Sir, I have packed twenty-three jars in straw and the empty one, marked Contentment, in my own shawl. We are to meet at the Kettle and Quill tea-room on Lantern Row at noon on Midwinter Day. You will know me by a brown coat and by the fact that I shall be arguing with the carrier about the straw.

One thing more, and then I shall seal this quickly. The day Mr. Tobble’s cart comes has become the best day in my month. I have checked my shelf, and I own no Salt that accounts for it. Do not answer that. Bring gloves. Emberwick is cold by the river.

volumes.title: Marrow and Vole
volumes.text:
Emberwick, Midwinter night. To Mrs. Grice, at Cold Ashby, from Dr. Ignatius Vole, who came here to settle with Miss Marrow of Saltmere whether the world is made of Salts or of Spirits.

Mrs. Grice, I shall not be home on Thursday. We met at noon and argued for one hour, to be polite. Then she set her empty jar on the table, the one marked Contentment, and I set my blue bottle beside it, and we forgot them and talked. At the third pot of tea she looked down. There were pale grains in the bottom of her jar. My bottle had gone misty. Neither of us will say whose came first.

The old books promise gold. We have taken a shop on Lantern Row instead. The sign is ordered: Marrow and Vole, Salts and Spirits. Please send the second chair by Mr. Tobble. You were right about it.

volumes.title: Note the First
volumes.text:
Barleyford, in the Lowlands, October. I am Fennel Ashdown, apprentice to Master Hob Tolliver, alchemist, whose workshop stands behind the wheelwright’s. Master’s eyes are not what they were, so from today I keep his notes.

Attempt the first of this book. Master set a brass bowl of rainwater on the south sill to gather a whole afternoon of sunlight, and had me stir it with a goose feather each time the clock struck. By evening the water was yellow. Yellow is not gold. Master says the difference between the two is the entire profession.

Mrs. Weld the dyer stopped and sniffed. She dipped a corner of her apron, looked at it, and bought the bowlful for two pennies. By market day there was wool on her stall the colour of marigolds. Master put the pennies in an old jar and had me label it. The label says Toward Gold.

volumes.title: The Shine Off a Penny
volumes.text:
Barleyford, November. Fennel Ashdown, apprentice, writing the notes of Master Hob Tolliver, alchemist. He has sought gold for forty years, and has me write down each attempt, since he can no longer read his own hand.

Attempt the second. Master reasoned that a new penny shines like gold, and that the shine must go somewhere. We sat a new penny among old ones in a covered dish and coaxed it. I was not told how one coaxes. Master hummed. After nine days we had a grey paste and a dull penny.

It was not gold. But I wiped my hands on the door latch, and the latch came up bright as a trumpet. Mr. Tapp from the inn took the whole pot for his horse brasses. You can now see the Barley Mow’s cart-horse coming from the far end of the Lowlands. Three pennies in the jar marked Toward Gold.

volumes.title: Frost and Candlelight
volumes.text:
Barleyford, in the Lowlands, December. I am Fennel Ashdown, and I keep the workshop notes for my master, Hob Tolliver, an alchemist whose sight is failing and whose hopes are not.

Attempt the third. Gold, says Master, is cold to the touch and warm to the eye. So we gathered frost from the water butt before dawn and held it near a candle for as long as it would stand. It would not stand long. What ran off into the dish dried to a thin clear skin, cracked all over like ice on a puddle.

Not gold. But Jessamy Marl the potter had come to borrow a sieve, and she turned the dish to the window. Her new jugs have that same crackle on them. She paid in pennies and a jug, and both stand on the shelf beside the jar marked Toward Gold.

volumes.title: A Pop and Some Soot
volumes.text:
Barleyford, January. Fennel Ashdown, apprentice to Master Hob Tolliver the alchemist, keeping his notes because his eyes cannot. We work behind the wheelwright’s, and the wheelwright has asked that today’s attempt at gold be recorded as his complaint also.

Attempt the fourth. Master wished to catch the gold that shows in a cat’s eyes by firelight. The cat was willing. The crucible was not. There was a pop, no louder than a cork, a smell of burnt toast, and a quantity of soot that went up to the rafters and came down on everything, the cat included. She has not been back.

No gold. I swept for an hour. But soot on a wet thumb writes, and writes very black. Miss Larkin the schoolmistress has taken a jarful for ink, and says her pupils’ blots have never been so handsome. This note is written in it.

volumes.title: The Intentions of Snowdrops
volumes.text:
Barleyford, in the Lowlands, February. I am Fennel Ashdown. My master, Hob Tolliver, is an alchemist with weak eyes and a strong will, and I write up his attempts at gold, of which this is the fifth.

Master holds that a snowdrop under the snow is a small white thing intending to be elsewhere, and that such intention might persuade lead to become gold. We filled a tub with earth from where the snowdrops grow thickest and kept it by the stove, speaking to it encouragingly. He did the speaking. In three weeks it was dark and crumbly and smelled of April.

The lead was unmoved. But old Mr. Hollin put his hand in the tub and would not take it out. He has dug it in along his south wall. He pays in pennies now and peas later, and the jar marked Toward Gold is a third full.

volumes.title: March Wind in a Bottle
volumes.text:
Barleyford, March. Fennel Ashdown, apprentice, keeping the notebook of Master Hob Tolliver, alchemist. He seeks gold; I write down what he finds in its place.

Attempt the sixth. Gold does not tarnish, Master says, because nothing can get a grip on it. Wind is the same. So we held bottles open on the hill above the mill in a March gale, corked them quickly, and shook them all the way home to keep the wind lively. Poured out, it was a grey gum that set in the dish while we were still looking at it. We have not got the spoon back.

It is not gold. It is, however, extremely firm. Mr. Felloe the wheelwright next door put a thumbful on a split spoke, and has since driven that wheel to Emberwick and back. He says he forgives us the soot of January. Six pennies and a pardon.

volumes.title: Rainbows in Eggshells
volumes.text:
Barleyford, in the Lowlands, April. I am Fennel Ashdown, apprentice. Master Hob Tolliver has spent forty years trying to make gold, and since his eyes dimmed I have kept the record. This is attempt the seventh.

Everyone knows what lies at a rainbow’s foot. Master proposed to save the walk. We set out forty eggshells in the yard to catch April rain while a rainbow stood over the mill, then stirred the shellfuls together with a goose feather and a great deal of hope. Overnight it thickened into a slippery grey cake.

There was no gold in it. There was, when I washed my hands afterwards, a lather up to my elbows. Mrs. Dabb the laundress heard by noon. She says the cake gets the mud out of a ploughman’s shirt in half the rubbing, and has ordered one a month. Master is rather hurt to be good at soap.

volumes.title: The Hum of a Hive
volumes.text:
Barleyford, May. Fennel Ashdown, apprentice to Master Hob Tolliver, alchemist. He can no longer see to write, so I set down each attempt at gold and what came of it. This is the eighth.

Bees make gold every summer and are not secretive about it. Master thought the secret was in the hum. We stood a jar beside Mr. Hollin’s hive with its mouth toward the noise, then stopped it and carried it home. Left by the stove, the jar gave us one pale candle. I cannot explain the wick.

It is not gold, though when lit it is the right colour at the top. It burns with a low steady sound and will not gutter in a draught. Mrs. Orchard the midwife carries one in her lantern on night calls. She paid eight pennies into the jar marked Toward Gold, and asked for another before autumn.

volumes.title: The Longest Day, Boiled Down
volumes.text:
Barleyford, in the Lowlands, Midsummer. I am Fennel Ashdown, and I keep the notes of my master, Hob Tolliver, who has been failing to make gold since before I was born. Attempt the ninth.

Master’s reasoning: the longest day holds the most sun, and gold is sun that has learned to sit still. We put a pan in the yard at first light and left the day to settle in it until the last light went. What had gathered came down to a spoonful of thick amber, which we did not taste. That is the first rule of this workshop.

Not gold. Sticky, though. Mr. Pippin of the orchard has painted a ring of it round each plum trunk, and the ants turn back like travellers at a toll gate. The jar marked Toward Gold is heavy now. I hear Master lift it when he thinks I am out.

volumes.title: A Bead of Almost-Glass
volumes.text:
Barleyford, July. Fennel Ashdown, apprentice, writing for Master Hob Tolliver, alchemist. This is the tenth attempt at gold in this notebook, and the first note I have not read back to him in full.

We set a pan of river sand on the sill to catch the flash of lightning. Afterwards there was one clear hard bead in it. Master held it to the window and asked me whether it was gold. He could not tell. I said no, Master. He nodded, and asked me to read him yesterday’s note, and then to read it again, slower.

A pedlar of spectacles came by and looked at the bead. Almost glass, he said, but not quite. He told me of a spectacle-maker in Emberwick who could give my master his own handwriting back, and he named the price. I counted the jar marked Toward Gold. It is not half enough.

volumes.title: The Cleanest Failure
volumes.text:
Barleyford, in the Lowlands, August. I am Fennel Ashdown, apprentice to Hob Tolliver the alchemist, whose eyes are too dim to read his own notes. This is attempt the eleventh, and a private matter besides.

The attempt first. Master set an empty crucible in the wheat field to take up the colour of the crop. In the evening it held nothing. He called it the cleanest failure of his life and seemed almost pleased.

The private matter. I told Mrs. Weld the dyer what a pair of spectacles costs, and how far short our jar fell. I only told her. By Friday the potter, the innkeeper, the schoolmistress, the wheelwright, the laundress, the midwife, old Mr. Hollin and Mr. Pippin had each come by with something in a fist. The jar marked Toward Gold will not close. I walk to Emberwick tomorrow. Master thinks I am visiting an aunt.

volumes.title: Gold, a Small Quantity
volumes.text:
Barleyford, September, harvest week. Fennel Ashdown, apprentice, with the last note in this book. My master, Hob Tolliver, has tried all year to make gold. Each failure was of use to some neighbour, and the neighbours’ pennies went into a jar.

I came back from Emberwick with what the jar bought: a pair of spectacles with gold rims. Half of Barleyford was in the yard. Master put them on and was quiet. Then he took this notebook and read it aloud, from the yellow water to the empty crucible, laughing in the right places. He looked at Mrs. Weld. He looked out at the wheat.

Then he gave the book back and dictated. Attempt the twelfth. Gold obtained at last, a small quantity, worn on the nose. Method: eleven failures and one village. He says it need not be repeated. He has read this line himself, and approves it.

volumes.title: The Heron Is Lit
volumes.text:
Reedham, at the edge of the marsh, January. I am Barnaby Withers, distiller. My still-house stands on stilts over the water, and my still is a copper vessel with a long bent neck that we call the Heron.

To distil is to warm a thing gently until the best of it rises, and then to catch that best as it cools and comes down. I do not make strong drink. I distil months. The old books say that twelve of them, joined, give the Quintessence, which mends all ills and may turn tin to gold.

January went into the pot this morning: frost scraped from the boardwalk, the tick of ice in the reeds, one note from a robin. By dusk I had a thimbleful, clear as glass. My neighbour Abel Coot, the old eel-catcher, sniffed the cork. “Cold iron and peat smoke,” he said. “That is January.”

volumes.title: A Thin Month
volumes.text:
The still-house at Reedham marsh, February. Barnaby Withers, distiller of months. I am drawing the essence of each month into a small bottle, twelve in all, to join at the year’s end into the Quintessence.

February is a thin month and gives little: rain on rope, grey light, a few hazel catkins. The second running gave nine drops. Abel Coot, my neighbour, came along the boardwalk to try it. His eyes show him only light and dark, but there is nothing amiss with his nose. “Wet doorstep,” he said. “And something just thinking of being green.”

I say the second running because I spoiled the first. I was impatient and built the peat fire too high under the Heron, my copper still, and all that came over was the smell of a scorched kettle. I began again with my hands in my pockets, where they could not meddle.

volumes.title: Wind in the Neck
volumes.text:
Reedham, on the marsh, March. I am Barnaby Withers, and my trade is distilling months: one small bottle from each, drawn off through a copper still called the Heron. Twelve bottles joined should make the Quintessence. This is the third.

March will not stay in the pot. I put in a gust from the east dyke, the slap of washing on a line and the mud beginning to wake, and each time I turned my back the lid lifted and the wind went out by the door. The Heron whistled through her neck like a boy calling a dog.

In the end I sat on the lid. What came down was cloudy and restless, and it will not lie still in the bottle. My neighbour, old Abel Coot, took one sniff and held on to his hat. I have put it on the shelf between February and a brick.

volumes.title: Seven Kinds of Rain
volumes.text:
The still-house on stilts, Reedham marsh, April. Barnaby Withers, distiller. Each month this year I draw the essence of the month into a bottle, hoping the twelve will make the Quintessence the old books promise.

April is mostly rain, but rain is not one thing. I set out seven cups and caught seven kinds: the fine sort that hangs, the sort that arrives sideways, the warm heavy drops before thunder, the sunlit sort the marsh children call a heron’s wedding, and three I have no names for. Into the Heron, my copper still, they went, with a cuckoo’s first call and the green that is on everything.

The bottle came out faintly green. I put one drop on a handkerchief and carried it to Abel Coot, the old eel-catcher, whose sight has nearly gone. He held it to his face. “Seven,” he said. I had not told him.

volumes.title: Too Much May
volumes.text:
Reedham, at the marsh edge, May. I am Barnaby Withers, and I distil months, one small bottle from each, through a long-necked copper still named the Heron. There will be twelve by the year’s end, and then I shall join them.

Every month has needed coaxing. May needed a bucket. I put in hawthorn blossom, the smell of the dyke bank in the sun and the noise of every bird at once, and the Heron ran like a gutter. I fetched a second, then a jug. The still-house smelled so strongly of May that the bees came in and would not be argued with.

I kept one small bottle, as the method requires, and poured the rest off the boardwalk into the marsh, which seemed pleased. Abel Coot, my neighbour, did not need to come and sniff. He called across from his doorstep: “I have it from here, thank you.”

volumes.title: June in a Bottle
volumes.text:
The still-house at Reedham marsh, June. Barnaby Withers, distiller of months. Five bottles stand on my shelf, and at the year’s end I mean to join twelve into the Quintessence. Today I drew off June.

It went into the Heron, my copper still, easily: warm boards, the south wind bringing hay from the Lowlands, eel-smoke, and the light that is still in the sky at ten. It came down slow and gold-coloured, the first that has had any colour.

I took it next door to Abel Coot. He was an eel-catcher for sixty years. Now his sight has gone and his knees with it, and he has not been further than his doorstep since the winter. He held June under his nose and told me about a hayfield he worked in at fourteen, and a dog called Button. He kept the bottle a long while. I did not hurry him.

volumes.title: Thunder Will Not Distil
volumes.text:
Reedham marsh, July. I am Barnaby Withers. I keep a copper still called the Heron in a house on stilts, and with her I am bottling the essence of each month this year, for a purpose the old books call the Quintessence.

I wanted the thunderstorm. It was the great event of July, purple from the coast to the Fells, and I had the pot ready with the lid off. Thunder will not distil. The noise went straight through the copper and out again, the lightning stayed outdoors, and the Heron sulked with her neck gone cold.

What I did catch was the quarter of an hour before: the hush, the smell of hot dust and of rain not yet arrived, a single swift. It made six heavy drops. I thought it a poor showing until Abel Coot, my neighbour, sniffed the cork and went to shut his window.

volumes.title: Abel Tests the Shelf
volumes.text:
The still-house on stilts, Reedham, August. Barnaby Withers, distiller. I have eight small bottles now, one for each month since January, and four to go before I may join them into the Quintessence.

Today I played a trick on my neighbour, Abel Coot, the old eel-catcher, who can no longer see the marsh he worked all his life. I shuffled the eight bottles and handed them to him unlabelled. He named every one. He had a story for each. February was his mother’s kitchen door. March was a kite. With June he was quiet, and smiled.

Then I did a thing the method does not ask for. From each bottle I drew a few drops into a phial the size of a thimble, corked it, and set the eight phials in a drawer. In case of breakage, I told the Heron. She is only a still, and did not argue.

volumes.title: Mist and Blackberries
volumes.text:
Reedham, at the edge of the marsh, September. I am Barnaby Withers, who distils months through a copper still called the Heron. Nine months are now in bottles, and December will bring the joining of all twelve.

September is the easiest month I have had. It wants to be kept. I put in the morning mist off the dyke, spiders’ webs with the dew on, blackberries and the first evening cool enough for a fire. The Heron hardly needed the peat. What came down was the colour of weak tea and smelled like the inside of a basket.

I filled the bottle, and a small phial besides, for I am keeping a second set and no longer pretend it is in case of breakage. Abel Coot, my old neighbour, had the phial uncorked by his chair all afternoon. He says it is like having the window open without the draught.

volumes.title: Leaf Smoke
volumes.text:
The still-house at Reedham marsh, October. Barnaby Withers, distiller of months. Ten bottles of twelve are filled, toward the Quintessence I mean to make at the year’s end.

October was bonfire smoke, apples laid out in a loft and the geese coming over at dusk, calling. It distilled dark and slow. I should have enjoyed it more, but Abel Coot, my neighbour, has been poorly and keeps to his chair. He is the old eel-catcher who names every month by its smell. He sent word that he could not manage the boardwalk, and would I bring October to him.

I did. I uncorked it by his elbow and said nothing. He turned his head toward the window, which was shut. “Geese,” he said. “Going over the east dyke. Late this year.” They were. I left the small bottle on his sill and walked back to the Heron in the dark.

volumes.title: The Fog Month
volumes.text:
Reedham, on the marsh, November. I am Barnaby Withers, and with a copper still called the Heron I am bottling the eleventh month of this year. One more, and I may join the twelve as the old books direct.

November nearly beat me. Fog walks into a pot willingly, but three times it came out as plain water, smelling of nothing. I had been taking the fog for the month. The month was what people do about the fog: wet wool by a stove, lamp oil, toast, a door shut quickly. That distilled at once. Abel Coot, my neighbour, sniffed it from his chair and asked who was making toast.

I have read the old books again. Twelve months joined, they say, give the Quintessence, cure for every ill. I note that not one of their authors appears to have lived on a marsh, or to have had a neighbour.

volumes.title: Twelve Bottles
volumes.text:
The still-house on stilts, Reedham marsh, Midwinter. Barnaby Withers, distiller. All year I have bottled the essence of each month, to join the twelve into the Quintessence.

December came over this morning: peat smoke, orange peel, cold stars. Then I poured all twelve into the great flask. It went the colour of dyke water and smelled of a Tuesday with nothing in it. A whole year at once, I find, is only weather.

But there was the second set. I carried twelve phials, in a box with twelve holes, along the boardwalk to Abel Coot, the old eel-catcher, who can no longer see or walk his marsh. He felt along the row and drew the sixth cork. The room had hay in it. He laughed, and sat in June for an hour with the snow coming down outside. The Heron is cold tonight. In January I begin again, two sets.
